prompt: Which storage type should hold a database's own data files?

options.text: Object storage
Block storage
A CDN
Email

explanation: Databases need low-latency random writes to a mounted volume.

prompt: What does object storage give up compared with a filesystem?

options.text: Durability, since objects keep fewer copies than disks
In-place updates, appends and renames of files
Direct access over HTTP from browsers and clients
Custom metadata attached alongside each stored file

explanation: Objects are written and replaced whole: there is no in-place edit, append or atomic rename (no POSIX semantics). Object storage is actually more durable than a single disk (many copies across zones), is accessed over HTTP, and supports per-object metadata.

options.text: A real directory that S3 creates and tracks
Just a key prefix; the namespace is flat
A separate bucket nested inside the parent
A storage class applied to a group of keys

explanation: The S3 namespace is flat; slashes are just characters in keys and the console shows shared prefixes as 'folders'. There is no directory object, no nested bucket, and storage class is set per object, not by folder.

scenario: A photo app stores images in a Postgres bytea column. The table is 14 TB, nightly backups take 9 hours, a new replica takes 3 days to build, and the cache hit rate for user rows has collapsed.

options.text: Add more read replicas so backups and reads spread across copies
Move images to object storage; keep only metadata rows in the DB
Compress the image bytes inside the table to shrink the 14 TB
Shard the images table by user ID across several Postgres nodes

explanation: Bytes belong in object storage and metadata (key, size, owner) in the database. Replicas copy all 14 TB again, shards spread the same bloat around, and images are already compressed formats so in-table compression barely helps.

prompt: What does a presigned URL let a client do?

options.text: Read any object in the bucket for as long as the key exists
Do one operation on one object directly, until it expires
Skip your API's authentication for all later requests too
Change the bucket policy so the object becomes public

explanation: A presigned URL is scoped to one method, one key and an expiry, signed by your service. It doesn't grant bucket-wide or permanent access, doesn't touch your API's auth, and can't change bucket policy.

scenario: App servers proxy every upload to object storage. During evening peaks they hit their network limits and slow mobile uploads hold thousands of connections open.

options.text: Scale app servers up to larger instances with more network bandwidth
Presigned URLs so clients upload straight to storage; API records metadata
Add a load balancer with sticky sessions so uploads spread more evenly
Re-encode images at lower quality on the server before forwarding them

explanation: Presigned uploads take the bytes out of the app path, so the API only issues URLs and records metadata. Bigger servers, sticky load balancing or server-side re-encoding all still pull every byte through the app tier.

prompt: Why use multipart upload for a 10 GB file?

options.text: It is the only upload method that lets you set custom metadata
Parts upload in parallel and a failure retries only one part
It encrypts each part separately, which a single PUT cannot do
It deduplicates the parts, so the stored object ends up smaller

explanation: Multipart gives parallelism and resumability: a failed part is retried alone (S3 also caps a single PUT at 5 GB). Metadata and encryption work on a normal PUT too, and parts are concatenated, not deduplicated.

prompt: What happens to an unfinished multipart upload's parts?

options.text: They are deleted automatically as soon as the client disconnects
They stay stored and billed until aborted; use a lifecycle rule
They become publicly readable because no object ACL applies yet
They are merged into a partial object after a short timeout

explanation: Uploaded parts sit (and are billed) until the upload is completed or aborted, so add a lifecycle rule to abort incomplete uploads. Nothing deletes or merges them automatically, and they are never exposed publicly.

scenario: To save money you moved all objects older than 7 days to an infrequent-access class. Analytics jobs read last month's files daily. The bill went up.

options.text: Archive tiers always cost more per GB than the standard class
IA classes charge per GB retrieved, and these files are read often
Lifecycle transitions copy objects, so you now pay for both copies
The CDN stops caching objects once they move to a colder class

explanation: Infrequent-access classes have cheaper storage but charge per GB retrieved (plus minimum durations), so daily-read files cost more there. Cold tiers are cheaper per GB stored, transitions don't leave a second billed copy, and storage class doesn't change CDN caching.

prompt: Why use content-hashed, versioned object keys behind a CDN?

options.text: Hashed keys are shorter, so CDN lookups and logs are cheaper
A changed file gets a new key, so long cache TTLs need no purges
CDNs refuse to cache objects whose keys carry no version marker
Hashing the key encrypts the file so the CDN cannot read it

explanation: Content-hashed keys are immutable: a new version gets a new URL, so long cache lifetimes are safe and no purge is needed. Key length doesn't matter, CDNs cache any key, and hashing a name encrypts nothing.
